title: Getting home from Mexico across the border at Brownsville
summary: Love gets a certificate in Monterey, travels through disrupted territory and is searched at Matamoros and Brownsville on the way home for Christmas.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: He got something to kick out of me. You said you went back to the council and said you got a...

Yeah, I went to the council and he gave me a card, a certificate, you know, a card that they wouldn't hold me up on the border. And he said, now listen, he says, they blowed up the track the other day in Victoria on the way to Monterey and said, you got a chance to go, said they're going to have some soldiers on the train. And I said, we can't guarantee you get there and say, if you want to take a chance, I told him, yeah, I want to take a chance because the band over there, you know, I scared it over there, everybody fighting. So he wrote out the certificate and he told me when I get to Monterey, I had to stop overnight anyhow, to continue to Matamoros the next morning. He said, the hotel right at the station, you go to American Hotel, get your room, he said, six o'clock in the morning when you get on the train going to the border, he said, they'll check your suitcase. They wiped all the marks off, you know, and checked my suitcase. So he said, now when you get to Matamoros, if they ask you why you come from this, tell them you just come from Monterey. And they asked you what you're doing down in Mexico, they're telling you was visiting and playing music at the same time, and you wanted to go home for Christmas. They thought you'd just go home. So they asked me, why you come from Monterey. He told me not to say nothing about Tick, Tamp, they might hold me up, Daniel, for a while.
So I let out for the border.

When I got there, on the Mexico side of the border, they have a Mexican there to search you again. I got there, they searched my baggage and everything. Then they let you go to the middle of the bridge there. They have a United States soldier and a Mexican soldier. You got to take your clothes off. And dress, go in another room and just go all through your clothes, you know. They do that on account of getting dope, you know. They catch people with dope coming from over there. And rip your tire open. And so I passed D9. When I got on the United States side, in Brownsville, Texas, I was satisfied then, you know. All American fellas, but they sure, they had to tell why you was born, how old you was, and who was your mother, your sisters, brothers. And they asked you, do you think you want to go back over there again, you know. I told them, well, I don't live over there. I live in the United States. I'm going home for Christmas. And I said, if I don't find a good job, I may go back over there and work some more. I might, but I said. I made up my mind whether I'm going back or not. I didn't want them to think I was scared, you know. But I was. I was so busy getting home. And you say, well, okay. And I was all right then. I went and got me some cars and rode home, you know, on the border.
